title: Navigation Math — TAS, Groundspeed, Headings, and Time/Distance/Fuel

questions.text: A pilot plans a 90-minute VFR day cross-country. The aircraft burns 9 gallons per hour at cruise. After accounting for startup, taxi, runup, and a full-power climb phase, the pilot calculates total trip fuel at 16 gallons. How many total gallons must be on board at departure to meet the minimum requirement of 14 CFR 91.151?

options.label: A
options.text: 25 gallons — 14 CFR 91.151 requires both a minimum 30-minute reserve and a mandatory fuel diversion margin of 30 minutes per leg; the pilot must carry 16 + 4.5 + 4.5 gallons to be legally compliant for any cross-country exceeding 50 nautical miles

options.label: B
options.text: 20.5 gallons — the 30-minute VFR day reserve at 9 GPH requires 4.5 gallons; added to the 16-gallon trip fuel, the legal minimum fuel at departure is 20.5 gallons total to comply with 14 CFR 91.151

options.label: C
options.text: 16 gallons — 14 CFR 91.151 requires fuel to reach the destination only; the 30-minute reserve is stored separately and does not need to be calculated separately from the trip fuel for departure planning purposes

options.label: D
options.text: 20.5 gallons — but the pilot must carry a second separate container of 4.5 gallons of fuel designated as the reserve, which may not be consumed during the flight until the destination is in sight and the landing approach has begun

questions.explanation: 14 CFR 91.151 requires fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing AND fly for at least 30 minutes more at normal cruising speed during the day. The 30-minute reserve at 9 GPH = 9 × 0.5 = 4.5 gallons. Total minimum: 16 (trip) + 4.5 (reserve) = 20.5 gallons total on board at departure. There is no regulatory requirement to carry the reserve in a separate container — the reserve is an accounting concept: the fuel that must remain usable after reaching the destination. A dual-reserve 'diversion margin' requirement does not exist in 91.151. The professional recommendation is to plan for 1 hour of reserve (9 gallons), bringing the total to 25 gallons — but the legal minimum is 20.5.

questions.text: A pilot in Atlanta, Georgia (Eastern Time zone) plans to depart at 10:00 AM local time during July (Daylight Saving Time in effect). The flight plan requires an ETE of 2 hours and 30 minutes. What is the destination ETA expressed in UTC?

options.label: A
options.text: 1630Z — Eastern Daylight Time (summer) is UTC minus 4 hours; adding 4 hours to 10:00 AM local gives 1400Z departure, plus 2 hours 30 minutes ETE gives 1630Z as the ETA

options.label: B
options.text: 1700Z — Eastern time is always UTC minus 5 hours regardless of season; Daylight Saving Time does not affect the UTC offset for aviation purposes because the FAA standardizes all time references on Standard Time year-round

options.label: C
options.text: 1730Z — Eastern Standard Time is UTC minus 5 hours; adding 5 hours to 10:00 AM local gives a 1500Z departure, plus 2 hours 30 minutes ETE gives 1730Z as the ETA

options.label: D
options.text: 1530Z — Atlantic Daylight Time applies in Georgia during July; Georgia observes UTC minus 3 hours in the summer, making 10:00 AM local equal to 1300Z departure and 1530Z ETA

questions.explanation: During Daylight Saving Time (approximately March through November), Eastern Daylight Time (EDT) is UTC − 4 hours. To convert local to UTC, add 4 hours: 10:00 AM EDT + 4 hours = 14:00 UTC (1400Z). Adding the 2 hour 30 minute ETE: 1400Z + 0230 = 1630Z. Using the Standard Time offset (UTC − 5) is incorrect during the summer months — this is the Daylight Saving Time trap the DPE exploits on checkrides. Inventing an Atlanta-specific Atlantic Daylight Time offset that does not exist is wrong — Georgia is Eastern. And the claim that the FAA standardizes on Standard Time year-round is false — aviation uses actual local Zulu time, which accounts for Daylight Saving.

questions.text: A pilot measures a True Course of 350° on the sectional. Winds aloft require a right crab of 6°. Magnetic variation in the area is 15° West. The compass deviation card shows +2° for the north quadrant heading. What is the Compass Heading?

options.label: A
options.text: 329° — TC 350° - 6° WCA (left crab) = TH 344°; subtract West variation: 344° - 15° = 329° MH; deviation is not applied in VFR navigation; final Compass Heading is 329°

options.label: B
options.text: 373° — TC 350° + 6° WCA = TH 356°; add West variation: 356° + 15° = 371° MH; add deviation: 371° + 2° = 373° CH; converted to compass value: 373° − 360° = 013° CH

options.label: C
options.text: 341° — TC 350° + 6° WCA = TH 356°; subtract West variation (East is least, West is best = subtract for West): 356° - 15° = 341° MH; no deviation applied because deviation is negligible on a VFR flight

options.label: D
options.text: 013° — TC 350° + 6° WCA = TH 356°; add West variation (West is best = add): 356° + 15° = 371° MH; add deviation +2°: 371° + 2° = 373°; 373° − 360° = 013° Compass Heading

questions.explanation: Step-by-step applying the TC → TH → MH → CH sequence: (1) TC = 350°. (2) TH = TC + WCA (right crab = right = add): 350° + 6° = 356° TH. (3) MH = TH ± Variation. Rule: West is Best → ADD West variation: 356° + 15° = 371° MH. (4) CH = MH ± Deviation. Deviation +2°: 371° + 2° = 373°. Converting 373° to a compass bearing: 373° − 360° = 013° Compass Heading. Subtracting West variation is incorrect (East is Least applies to East variation — West variation is added). Applying the WCA in the wrong direction (the problem states a right crab = add to TC, not subtract) and skipping deviation is also wrong. Deviation is always applied — it is not negligible.

questions.text: A pilot is cruising at 8,500 feet MSL with an indicated airspeed of 100 knots. The winds aloft at 9,000 feet show a 15-knot headwind on the planned course. Approximately what groundspeed should the pilot use for navlog ETE calculations?

options.label: A
options.text: 101 knots — TAS is calculated by adding 2% of IAS per 1,000 feet above sea level: at 8,500 feet, TAS ≈ 100 × 1.17 = 117 knots; subtract 15-knot headwind: 117 - 15 = 102 knots; round to 101 knots for navlog purposes

options.label: B
options.text: 117 knots — True Airspeed is the only correct value for groundspeed calculations; wind components are incorporated separately after landing by comparing planned ETA to actual arrival time, not during preflight navlog calculations

options.label: C
options.text: 102 knots — TAS at 8,500 feet with IAS of 100 knots is approximately 117 knots (2% per 1,000 feet × 8.5); subtracting the 15-knot headwind yields a groundspeed of approximately 102 knots for ETE calculations

options.label: D
options.text: 85 knots — IAS is the appropriate airspeed for time-enroute calculations because the airspeed indicator displays the operationally relevant speed that ATC uses for traffic separation; subtract the headwind component from IAS: 100 - 15 = 85 knots groundspeed

questions.explanation: The correct calculation: (1) Convert IAS to TAS: at 8,500 feet, apply approximately 2% per 1,000 feet increase: 8.5 × 2% = 17% increase. TAS ≈ 100 × 1.17 = 117 knots. (2) Apply wind: 15-knot headwind = subtract: 117 − 15 = 102 knots groundspeed. (3) Use groundspeed (102 knots) for all ETE and fuel calculations. Using IAS − wind understates groundspeed because IAS does not account for altitude TAS increase — producing an ETE that is too long and a fuel burn that is recalculated incorrectly. The 101-knot answer arrives at essentially the same result as the correct 102-knot groundspeed but rounds to 101. Treating TAS (117 knots) as groundspeed and deferring wind application to post-flight is incorrect — this is operationally dangerous because wind affects actual fuel burn.

questions.text: During preflight, a pilot checks the fuel gauges and both show 3/4 full on a 40-gallon aircraft, suggesting 30 gallons. The planned cross-country requires 22 gallons including a 45-minute reserve (night flight). Should the pilot use this reading and depart?

options.label: A
options.text: Yes — 30 gallons of fuel is sufficient to complete a 22-gallon trip with an 8-gallon margin; FAA-certified fuel gauges are required to be accurate by law and a 3/4 reading on both tanks is a reliable indication for flight planning purposes

options.label: B
options.text: No — fuel gauges are prohibited from being used for any flight planning purpose under 14 CFR 91.103; all cross-country fuel calculations must be based exclusively on fueling receipts from the most recent full fuel load regardless of current gauge readings

options.label: C
options.text: No — 14 CFR 23.1337 only requires fuel quantity gauges to be accurate when reading zero (empty); a 3/4 gauge reading does not guarantee 30 gallons are physically present; the pilot must visually measure fuel using a calibrated dipstick before departure for a 22-gallon night flight

options.label: D
options.text: Yes — for cross-country flights under 100 nautical miles, FAA guidance permits the use of fuel gauge indications when both gauges agree with each other; disagreement between gauges would require dipstick verification, but matching readings are operationally reliable

questions.explanation: 14 CFR 23.1337 requires fuel quantity indicators to be accurate only when they read zero (empty). All positive fuel gauge readings are approximations that can vary significantly from actual fuel quantities due to sensor calibration drift, fuel expansion, aircraft pitch attitude, and manufacturing tolerances. A 3/4 gauge on a 40-gallon aircraft could represent anywhere from 27 to 33 gallons in practice. For a 22-gallon night flight (which requires a 45-minute reserve under 91.151), the only reliable method is to physically measure fuel using a calibrated dipstick during preflight. The claim that FAA gauges are legally accurate at all readings is false. The invented 100 nm distance threshold and 'matching gauge' exception has no basis in 23.1337 or 91.103. And treating gauges as prohibited from all flight planning overstates the prohibition — gauges may be referenced as supplemental information, but cannot be the sole fuel planning basis.

questions.text: A pilot calculates an En Route Time (ETE) of 1 hour and 45 minutes. The departure time is 14:30 local (Eastern Standard Time, UTC-5). What is the UTC ETA?

options.label: A
options.text: 2115Z — convert 14:30 EST to UTC by adding 5 hours: 14:30 + 5:00 = 19:30Z; add ETE 1 hour 45 min (1.75 hours = 1 hour 75 minutes): 19:30 + 1:75 = 21:15Z = 2115Z

options.label: B
options.text: 2130Z — convert 14:30 EST to UTC by adding 5 hours: 1930Z departure; add ETE 2 hours (rounding 1 hour 45 minutes up to the next full hour for conservative SAR planning): 1930 + 0200 = 2130Z

options.label: C
options.text: 2045Z — convert 14:30 EST to UTC by adding 5 hours: 1930Z departure; add ETE 1 hour 15 minutes (incorrectly converting 1.75 hours to 1:15): 1930 + 0115 = 2045Z

options.label: D
options.text: 2115Z — convert 14:30 EST to UTC by adding 5 hours: 14:30 + 5:00 = 1930Z; add ETE 1 hour 45 minutes: 1930Z + 0145 = 2115Z

questions.explanation: Two-step calculation: (1) UTC conversion: Eastern Standard Time is UTC − 5 hours. Add 5 hours to convert local to UTC: 14:30 local + 5:00 = 19:30Z departure (1930Z). (2) Add ETE: 1 hour 45 minutes = 0145 in time arithmetic (base 60). 1930Z + 0145 = 21:15Z = 2115Z. The answer that reaches the same final result (2115Z) but describes 1.75 hours as '1 hour 75 minutes' performs an incorrect intermediate step — a base-10/base-60 confusion; while the final number happens to be correct in this case, the method is wrong and will produce errors in other scenarios. The answer that treats 0.75 hours as 15 minutes demonstrates the classic base-10 conversion error (quarter of 60 = 15 is correct in this case, but the methodology described is incorrect — 1.75 hours = 1 hr 45 min, not 1 hr 15 min). The answer that rounds up to a full hour for conservative planning is not the standard ETA calculation method.

questions.text: Airborne 45 minutes into a 2-hour cross-country, the pilot notices the groundspeed is 80 knots instead of the planned 100 knots due to an unforecast 20-knot headwind. Original fuel load: 30 gallons. Cruise burn: 9 GPH. What is the SAFEST action?

options.label: A
options.text: Recalculate the total revised ETE using the actual groundspeed, compute remaining fuel at destination, verify whether legal reserve will be maintained, and divert to an intermediate fuel stop if the revised calculations show less than 30 minutes of reserve remaining

options.label: B
options.text: Continue to the destination — the aircraft departed with 30 gallons and only 45 minutes have elapsed; even at the reduced groundspeed the aircraft has sufficient fuel to complete the trip within the 30-minute reserve requirement

options.label: C
options.text: Declare a fuel emergency immediately and request ATC divert assistance — any unforecast headwind greater than 15 knots constitutes a fuel emergency under 14 CFR 91.151 that legally requires immediate ATC notification and landing at the nearest suitable airport

options.label: D
options.text: Increase engine power to maximum continuous and fly at maximum IAS — increasing airspeed by 15 knots will mostly offset the 20-knot headwind and restore the planned groundspeed without requiring a divert or additional fuel stop

questions.explanation: The correct action is to recalculate in real time. At 45 minutes with 9 GPH burn: 6.75 gallons used, leaving 23.25 gallons. With actual GS of 80 knots, the revised ETE for the remaining distance must be recalculated. If the original plan was 200 nm at 100 knots (2 hours), after 45 minutes at 80 knots the aircraft has covered 60 nm, leaving approximately 140 nm. At 80 knots: 140 ÷ 80 = 1.75 hours more. Total fuel burn remaining: 1.75 × 9 = 15.75 gallons. Fuel at destination: 23.25 − 15.75 = 7.5 gallons = about 50 minutes of reserve. In this specific example the math works — but the key lesson is that the pilot MUST recalculate dynamically at each checkpoint rather than assuming preflight calculations remain valid. Continuing to the destination on the original plan is Invulnerability — trusting the original fuel plan without recalculating for a 20% groundspeed reduction. Increasing engine power to maximum is Get-There-Itis — burning more fuel at higher power is self-defeating against a headwind. Declaring an immediate fuel emergency misstates the law — an unforecast headwind alone is not a fuel emergency.
questions.sjt_rationale: Continuing on the original plan is Invulnerability — ignoring a significant deviation from the fuel plan. Increasing power to outrun the headwind is Get-There-Itis — trying to outrun the problem with power rather than evaluating. Declaring a fuel emergency is Resignation — over-escalating to a fuel emergency without completing a revised calculation first. Recalculating and verifying margins is correct ADM: recalculate, verify margins, divert if margins are insufficient.

questions.text: A student pilot presents a navlog to a CFI. The CFI notices the student used their magnetic HEADING (which accounts for a significant crosswind correction) instead of the magnetic COURSE when applying the 91.159 VFR cruising altitude rule. The planned altitude is therefore incorrect. The student says 'they're close enough.' What is the appropriate response?

options.label: A
options.text: Approve the flight with a deferred correction — note the error in the student's logbook as a training item and brief the student to correct the altitude once airborne by requesting a non-standard VFR altitude from ATC if needed

options.label: B
options.text: Correct the altitude to the legally required value based on the magnetic COURSE, update the navlog, and use this as a teaching moment to explain that the 91.159 altitude system provides passive vertical IFR/VFR separation that only works when all pilots apply the rule correctly using course, not heading

options.label: C
options.text: Allow the flight to proceed — if the difference between heading and course is less than 20 degrees, the altitude difference is often one level only (500 feet); flying at the wrong cruising altitude by one level does not create a measurably higher collision risk with IFR traffic

options.label: D
options.text: Cancel the flight entirely — using the wrong value in the 91.159 altitude calculation is a deliberate falsification of the navlog that constitutes grounds for certificate action under 14 CFR 61.59 and requires a written safety report before further training can proceed

questions.explanation: The correct response is to fix the error before flight and explain the regulatory and safety basis. The NEODD/SWEVEN cruising altitude rule under 91.159 works because ALL aircraft using opposing courses fly at different altitude strata — but only if everyone applies the rule correctly using COURSE, not HEADING. Using a slightly wrong quadrant puts the aircraft at an altitude stratum where opposing VFR traffic is expected from the same direction — eliminating the passive separation the rule provides. Allowing the flight to proceed is Macho — rationalizing a known regulatory violation with a 'close enough' standard. Approving the flight with a deferred in-flight correction is Resignation — deferring a safety correction to in-flight when ground correction is available. Cancelling the flight outright dramatically overreacts — a navlog calculation error is a training deficiency, not certificate fraud.
questions.sjt_rationale: Allowing the flight is Macho — minimizing a systematic error because the consequence seems distant. Approving the flight with a deferred correction is Resignation — approving a flight with a known deficiency and deferring correction. Cancelling the flight catastrophizes a training error into a legal violation. Correcting the altitude before flight is the correct CFI response: correct the error, explain the system dependency.
